title: Haridasa Thakura
html:
The Namacharya

Krishnadasa Kaviraja, listing the branches of the tree of Chaitanya, speaks of him thus:

“Haridasa Thakura, another branch, lived a wondrous life: without fail he chanted three hundred thousand names every day. His virtues are endless; I can give only a glimpse of them. It was he whom Advaita Acharya fed from the plate of the memorial offering, the shraddha-patra. The waves of his virtues were like Prahlada's: even when the Yavanas beat him, he did not so much as frown. When he attained perfection, Chaitanya Prabhu took his body in His arms and danced in great joy.” (CC, Adi 10.43–46)

These four verses hold his whole life: the holy name, never abandoned; Advaita's love; patience under the canes; and a departure in the Lord's arms. The “Charitamrita” and the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” call him simply Haridasa or Thakura Haridasa; Murari Gupta calls him “the sage Haridasa”; the “Advaita-prakasha” and the “Prema-vilasa,” “Brahma-Haridasa.” The biographies name him Sri Haridasa Thakura, the saint, and the Namacharya — the teacher of the holy name.1 He is one of those eternal associates whom Krishna, as the “Charitamrita” says, sent into the world before Himself (Adi 13.52–55): Haridasa was born in a Muslim home in order to serve the Lord who was to come.2

Brahma and Prahlada

Who he is in eternity, Kavi Karnapura tells us:

“The son of the sage Richika, named Brahma, a great ascetic, was born together with Prahlada [in one person] and became the one called Haridasa. As the feet of Murari Gupta have said in the ‘Chaitanya-charitamrita’: the sage's son, bringing tulasi leaves in the morning unwashed, was cursed by his father and became a yavana; and he became Haridasa, endowed with supreme devotion.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 93–95)3

There is another account of why Brahma was born in a low family. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura gives it in the “Navadvipa-dhama-mahatmya”: Brahma, who had once stolen Krishna's calves and cowherd friends, feared to offend the Lord again when He came as Gauranga, and sat in meditation on Antardvipa. Gauranga appeared to him and said, “When I come as Gaura, you will be born in a family of mlecchas and will preach the glory of the holy name.” According to one of the biographies, the “Advaita-vilasa” tells the same; the “Advaita-prakasha,” the “Prema-vilasa” and the “Gaura-krishnodaya” (1.44–49) also speak of Brahma becoming Haridasa. It is said, too, that Brahma himself begged Krishna for birth in a low family, so that in Gaura's pastimes pride would not touch him. Birth among the Yavanas was not a punishment in the worldly sense but lila: by the Lord's will an eternal associate appeared where his humility and the glory of the holy name could be seen by all.

Those who lived with the Lord saw Brahma in him too. Lochana Dasa tells how once, as Haridasa danced before the Lord, Brahma manifested in him:

“Dancing and dancing, [Haridasa], in whom Brahma manifested, falls at the Lord's feet and prostrates; with four mouths, reciting the Vedas, he offers praise. ‘Be calm!’ says the Lord, lifts him up and embraces him.” (“Chaitanya-mangala,” Madhya, 30.31–32)

Kavi Karnapura says the same in his mahakavya (7.70–75). And Vrindavana Dasa records what the Vaishnavas of Navadvipa said: “One Vaishnava said, ‘Haridasa is like four-headed Brahma.’ Another said, ‘He is an incarnation of Prahlada’” (CB, Madhya 10.106).

Prahlada, son of the demon Hiranyakashipu, Haridasa resembles in his whole life. Vrindavana Dasa explains why he was born in a low family:

“By the Lord's will Haridasa was born in a family of low standing, to show that noble birth and high position in society have no real worth. Even if a devotee of the Lord is born in a low family, he is worthy of worship: this is the conclusion of the scriptures. If one born in a noble family does not worship the lotus feet of Sri Krishna, his high birth will not help him, and he will go to hell. To confirm the words of the scriptures Haridasa was born in a humble family.” (CB, Adi 16.237–240)

In Vrindavana Dasa these words are spoken by the King of serpents through the mouth of a snake charmer (of whom more below). And elsewhere: “Prahlada was born in a family of demons, Hanuman in a troop of monkeys, and in the same way Haridasa came into the world in a family of low origin” (CB, Madhya 10.111). One of the biographies adds that all three — Hanuman among the beasts, Prahlada among the asuras and Haridasa among the mlecchas — are teachers of the world.

Birthplace and Family

The “Chaitanya-bhagavata” names his birthplace:

“Haridasa Thakura was born in the village of Budhana, and for that reason Krishna is glorified there to this day.” (CB, Adi 16.18)

Budhana lay in the district of Jessore, now in Bangladesh; Haridasa appeared there more than five centuries ago. Where exactly it was is unclear today. According to one of the biographies, the name Budhana (Burhan) now belongs to a whole administrative area of the Satkhira subdivision of Khulna district; some look for the village in the Twenty-four Parganas, in West Bengal, others in Jessore; and since on the railway from Bongaon to Khulna Benapole comes next, Budhana probably lies on the far side of today's border.

He was born in a Muslim family: so say the “Chaitanya-bhagavata,” the “Charitamrita” and the “Chaitanya-mangala,” written almost in his own time, and so the biographies hold. Later sources tell it otherwise, but we keep their accounts to the notes.4 The original sources give neither his parents' names nor the year or day of his appearance; nor is the day of his appearance found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math. From early childhood he was attached to the name of Hari, and wherever the name was sung, there he could be found.

Benapole

According to tradition, as a young man Haridasa met a Vaishnava sadhu, and that company turned him away from worldly life. He lived with the sadhu for a long time, and then, on his instruction, built himself a hut of leaves in the forest near Benapole — far from Budhana, but in the same region.5 The “Charitamrita” tells:

“When Haridasa left his home, he lived for some time in the forest of Benapola. He built a hut in the solitary forest, served Tulasi, and night and day chanted three hundred thousand names. He lived on alms taken in brahmanas' houses, and by his spiritual power he won the reverence of all the people.” (CC, Antya 3.98–100)

The whole district belonged to the landlord Ramachandra Khan, a hater of Vaishnavas; he lived nearby, at a place that some know as Kagaja Pukuriya. People only feared him, while they honoured a mendicant hermit — and this he could not bear. He tried in one way and another to disgrace Haridasa, but could find no fault in him.

The Prostitute

Then Khan resolved to ruin the saint through a woman's charms and expose him as a hypocrite. He summoned prostitutes and promised them money and gifts if they could break the hermit's vow. The women themselves revered the Thakura as a great saint and feared to bring God's anger upon themselves, but Khan's money and fear of his men were stronger. One of them, young and beautiful, came forward: “In three days I shall captivate his mind” (CC, Antya 3.105).6 Khan wanted to send a constable with her to seize the saint on the spot, but she asked to go alone first; Khan's men could come with her later.

In the evening, adorned and perfumed, she came to the hut, bowed to the tulasi at the entrance, bowed to the Thakura and sat on the threshold. Uncovering part of her body, she said sweetly that she could not live without so handsome a young man. Haridasa answered her calmly:

“Haridasa said, ‘I shall accept you. But until I have finished chanting my fixed number of names, sit here and listen to the sankirtana of the name. When my chanting is finished, I shall do as you wish.’” (CC, Antya 3.113–114)

She stayed and waited, and he sang the name all night until dawn. In the morning she left and told Khan that the saint had already agreed. On the second night the same thing happened; Haridasa explained that he had vowed to chant ten million names (koti) in a month, and tomorrow the vow would be complete. On the third night, listening to the name, she herself began to repeat, “Hari! Hari!”

“As he chanted, the night came to an end; and through the Thakura's company the prostitute's heart was transformed. She fell flat at the Thakura's feet and confessed Ramachandra Khan's plot.” (CC, Antya 3.129–130)

She begged for mercy, and Haridasa told her:

“‘I know all about Khan's plot. He is an ignorant fool, and I feel no grief on his account. I would have left this place that very day; I stayed three days for your sake.’” (CC, Antya 3.132–133)

Not for a moment was the Thakura “tempted”: his promise “I shall accept you” was only a stratagem of compassion, so that for three nights she would hear the name and be purified.

He instructed her:

“‘Give away the goods of your house to brahmanas, and then come and live in this hut. Chant the name constantly and serve Tulasi. Then you will very soon attain the feet of Krishna.’ Saying this, he instructed her in chanting the name. Then the Thakura rose and departed, calling, ‘Hari! Hari!’” (CC, Antya 3.135–137)

She gave away all her property, shaved her head, kept a single cloth and, like her guru, chanted three hundred thousand names every day, served Tulasi and ate sparingly. With her senses subdued, she attained love for Krishna:

“She became a renowned and most exalted Vaishnavi, and great Vaishnavas would go to see her.” (CC, Antya 3.141)7

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati remarks in his “Anubhashya” on this account (Antya 3.139) that a guru, though entitled to all of a disciple's property, does not take it for himself; a Vaishnava guru stays free of the disciple's gift and teaches him to give up worldly pride, not to accept what the disciple has renounced. So does a pure devotee purify and uplift the fallen: like Jagai and Madhai by the mercy of Gaura and Nityananda, like the robber Ratnakara, who became Valmiki by the mercy of Narada. The people honoured the Thakura still more, and Ramachandra Khan burned with spite.

The Fate of Ramachandra Khan

The “Charitamrita” tells how the offence against the saint ended. Khan grew still more hostile to the Vaishnavas, and when Nityananda, preaching through Bengal, stopped at his house in the pavilion of Durga, Khan had Him told to lodge in a cowshed. Nityananda left, saying that this house was fit only for cow-killers. Soon a Muslim vizier descended on Khan for unpaid revenue: for three days he slaughtered cows in Durga's shrine, plundered the house and the village, and led Khan away with his family, depriving him of caste, wealth and people. Kaviraja concludes:

“Wherever a great soul is dishonoured, in a land or a village, the whole land is laid waste for the fault of a single person.” (CC, Antya 3.163)8

A Vaishnava bears no grudge against anyone and regards every suffering as the fruit of his own past, but Krishna does not tolerate offences against His devotees, and the fruit of an offence comes — sooner or later.

Chandapur

From Benapole Haridasa came to Chandapur, near today's Saptagram station, not many miles from the Bandel railway junction (Hooghly district). There he lived with Balarama Acharya, a disciple of Advaita and priest of the wealthy Majumdar brothers, Hiranya and Govardhana, revenue collectors of that district. Balarama had received Haridasa's mercy and was devoted to him; Haridasa chanted the name in a secluded thatched hut and took his meals in Balarama's house.9

“Raghunatha Dasa, then a boy at his studies, would go to see Haridasa Thakura. Haridasa bestowed his mercy upon him, and that mercy became the cause of his attaining Chaitanya.” (CC, Antya 3.168–169)

So exclusive devotion was planted as a seed in the heart of the future Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami.

One day, at the brothers' request, Balarama brought Haridasa to their house, to an assembly of learned brahmanas. The Majumdars rose to greet him, bowed and seated him in the place of honour; the guests praised him, and since the Thakura chanted three hundred thousand names a day, the talk turned to the glory of the holy name. Some said that the name destroys sins, others that it grants liberation. Haridasa objected:

“‘These two are not the fruit of the name. The fruit of the name is that love for Krishna's feet arises.’” (CC, Antya 3.177)

And he explained: before sunrise, while the sun is still below the horizon, the darkness already begins to lift and the fear of thieves and ghosts passes away.

“‘In the same way, as the name begins to rise, sins and the like are destroyed; when it has risen, love for Krishna's feet dawns. Liberation is a trifling fruit that comes from the mere semblance of the name (namabhasa). Krishna wishes to give that liberation, but His devotee does not accept it.’” (CC, Antya 3.184–185)

At the assembly was the brahmana Gopala Chakravarti, a fine-looking young scholar, the chief tax collector, who gathered twelve lakhs of coins for the Padishah.10 He could not bear to hear that liberation comes from the mere semblance of the name (namabhasa); leaping up, he exclaimed that these were the words of a sentimentalist: even by knowledge of Brahman liberation is not attained in ten million births. Haridasa calmly replied that all the scriptures say so. Then the brahmana demanded an oath:

“The brahmana said, ‘If liberation does not come from the semblance of the name, then pledge that you will cut off your nose!’ Haridasa said, ‘If liberation does not come from the semblance of the name, then I shall cut off my own nose — that is certain.’” (CC, Antya 3.196–197)11

The assembly was outraged. The Majumdars rebuked the brahmana and dismissed him from service, and Hiranya forbade him his door; Balarama told him, “You have insulted Haridasa Thakura! You will be utterly ruined; no good will come to you” (CC, Antya 3.200). All fell at the Thakura's feet, and he, smiling, reassured them:

“‘None of you is at fault, nor is this ignorant brahmana to blame: his mind is devoted to logic. The greatness of the name lies beyond the reach of logic. How could he know these truths? Go home. May Krishna bless you all, and may no one suffer on my account.’” (CC, Antya 3.203–205)

Within three days the brahmana was struck by leprosy: his nose and his fingers and toes fell away. Everyone saw how dear the Thakura was to the Lord. Haridasa himself wished no punishment:

“It is the nature of a devotee to forgive the faults of the ignorant; it is Krishna's nature that He cannot bear blasphemy of His devotee.” (CC, Antya 3.211)

The news of the brahmana's illness grieved Haridasa deeply; he took leave of Balarama and went to Shantipura, to Advaita.

With Advaita

Haridasa came to the Ganga, to Phulia — not far from Shantipura, where Sri Advaita Acharya lived.12 Phulia still stands on the railway between Ranaghat and Shantipura, about five miles north of Ranaghat.

“After some time Haridasa moved to the bank of the Ganga, to the village of Phulia near Shantipura. Meeting Haridasa, Advaita Acharya was boundlessly happy; in spiritual bliss He cried out aloud.” (CB, Adi 16.19–20)

He roamed the banks of the Ganga, chanting the name aloud: now he danced, now laughed, now roared like a lion; tears ran over his body, he trembled, his hair stood on end, and at times he fell senseless. The brahmanas of Phulia recognized him as a true saint and gave him a gopha — a little cave-cell in the shade of the trees.

In Advaita's assembly (one of the biographies places it in Navadvipa-Mayapur) Haridasa met Srivasa and the other Vaishnavas, who all rejoiced to see him. Advaita grieved that people had turned away from God and that the Lord was still delaying; the Vaishnavas discussed the Gita and the “Bhagavatam” and sang kirtana, which most people mocked. Haridasa was drawn by Advaita's talks on Vaishnava philosophy, and Advaita recognized in him a bhajanandi who never let go of the name.

“On the bank of the Ganga He made a secluded cave-dwelling for him, and He explained to him the devotional meaning of the ‘Bhagavata’ and the ‘Gita.’ Haridasa took his alms daily at the Acharya's house, and together the two of them relished talks about Krishna.” (CC, Antya 3.214–215)

Haridasa was uneasy: Advaita lived among high-born brahmanas, yet He fed and honoured one born in a Muslim family — might He not bring public censure on Himself? Advaita replied that He acted by the scriptures, not by rumour:

“‘Do not be afraid. I shall act only as the scriptures direct. When you eat, it is as good as feeding ten million brahmanas.’ Saying this, He fed him the shraddha-patra, the food of the day of shraddha.” (CC, Antya 3.219–220)

The shraddha-patra, the chief dish of the memorial meal, is by custom offered to the worthiest brahmana; Advaita offered it to Haridasa at the yearly shraddha for His ancestors, for, as one of the biographies says, there was no worthier brahmana in the whole district. From then on Haridasa ate at Advaita's house every day, and this was still before the Lord's appearance.13 A Vaishnava is worthy of honour whatever family he was born in — and for Advaita fidelity to scripture stood above the caution of caste.

From then on Haridasa was almost always with Advaita — now in Shantipura, now in Navadvipa-Mayapur, now in his cave in Phulia — and in his wanderings he showed people the worth of the holy name by his conduct and his words. No wonder the Lord later “complained” that Advaita, having called Him into the world, lived carefree with Haridasa in Shantipura.

Twenty-two Marketplaces

The kazi of that district lodged a complaint with the Badshah, the ruler of Gauda: one born a Muslim was following Hindu ways. The kazi feared that others would follow Haridasa and demanded swift punishment. Haridasa was arrested.

In prison the inmates, knowing of his holiness, hoped that by his blessing they would soon be released. He blessed them: “Stay as you are,” and, seeing their dismay, explained:

“Understand, I did not bless you to remain in prison. My words meant this: ‘Go on abstaining from enjoyment and always chant the holy name of Hari.’ Do not grieve, and do not think that I gave you a blessing with a double meaning.” (CB, Adi 16.63–64)

The Badshah, seeing the extraordinary radiance of his body, seated him in the place of honour and courteously asked why he, honoured with birth as a Muslim, followed the Hindus; let him recite the kalima and wash away his sin. Haridasa replied that God is one for all: only by the customs of different lands is He called by different names and worshipped with different rites; the same Lord dwells in every heart, and he acts as the Lord directs his mind; nor do the Hindus persecute a Hindu who adopts Muslim ways. “If this is a crime, punish me,” he said. This was an answer to a Muslim ruler, not a teaching that all paths are alike; Haridasa himself served Krishna's name alone. The Muslims present were satisfied, but the kazi demanded punishment: “This shaitan will make shaitans of others too.”

The Badshah again ordered him to recite the kalima, or else the kazi would punish him, and Haridasa answered:

“Even if my body is cut to pieces and I lose my life, I shall never stop chanting the holy name of the Lord.” (CB, Adi 16.94)14

So one who knows himself to be a soul places the soul above the body. The kazi pronounced the sentence: to be beaten with canes in twenty-two marketplaces until he gave up his life (CB, Adi 16.96); if he survived, it would mean that there was power in him and that he was right. Without waiting for the Badshah's seal, the kazi ordered it carried out.

He was led mercilessly from market to market, and he joyfully repeated, “Krishna, Krishna!” — and his body showed no sign of pain.

“In the same way Haridasa felt no pain when the Muslims beat him mercilessly.” (CB, Adi 16.110)

So once Prahlada did not feel the torments his father inflicted on him — the “Charitamrita” too compares Haridasa to Prahlada (Adi 10.45). An ordinary man would not have survived two or three markets. The people around suffered at the sight, and some slipped money to the executioners so that they would strike more lightly. And Haridasa prayed for his tormentors:

“‘O Krishna, be merciful to these souls! Forgive their offences. Do not punish them for tormenting me.’” (CB, Adi 16.113)

This was not martyrdom in the worldly sense but a revelation of his forbearance and of his mercy to those who wronged him. The executioners grew tired and were amazed that he was alive and at times even smiling: was he not a pir? In fear they said that if he stayed alive, the kazi would put them to death. Then the Thakura replied that since his life threatened them with death, he would leave his body at once — and he entered samadhi: no movement, no breath.

He was taken for dead and brought to the Badshah, who ordered him buried; but the kazi objected that burial would do him good and ordered him thrown into the Ganga. The current carried him away, and soon he was near Phulia; coming to himself, he walked out onto the bank, chanting the name aloud.15

Everyone was astonished, especially the kazi's men, and they bowed to him as a true saint. The Badshah too came, bowed and begged forgiveness — and received it. Haridasa was allowed to chant the name and go wherever he wished, and no one dared hinder him again.16 To the saint all were equal: he wished no punishment on his tormentors and did not regard them as enemies.

He entered Phulia chanting the name. The brahmanas, stunned by the news of his sufferings, rejoiced and cried, “Hari! Hari!” Hearing the name after a long interval, Haridasa began to dance — with tears, trembling and swoons — and he told the brahmanas not to grieve: his suffering was the fruit of his own offence, for he had heard blasphemy against God, and the punishment was even mild. So humbly did he explain his lot. Later, at the Mahaprakasha, the Lord revealed to him what had happened to the Lord Himself that day (of which more below).17

The Serpent in the Cave

Afterwards Haridasa came to have a gopha — a small underground cell for one, where he could remember Krishna in solitude and chant his three hundred thousand names; the cell became like Vaikuntha. But at its bottom lived a huge serpent, and its poisonous breath burned the bodies of all who entered; visitors could not stay long, while Haridasa himself noticed nothing.

The brahmanas discussed this burning, and experts in snakebite said that a large serpent lived inside; they urged Haridasa to move. He replied, “It is no hardship for me here, but I cannot bear your suffering: if the serpent does not leave, tomorrow I shall,” — and went on singing Krishna's glories.

Learning of this, the serpent crawled out of the cell of its own accord at dusk and went away. Everyone saw how huge and mottled it was — yellow, blue and white — and a jewel shone on its head; the brahmanas chanted Krishna's name in fear. The burning stopped, and the reverence for the Thakura grew a hundredfold.18

The Danka

Once a snake charmer with his troupe — they earned their living by dancing to music — was giving a performance at a palace; among them was a man possessed by a serpent (a danka). They sang “The Subduing of Kaliya,” and the danka danced in time. Haridasa happened to be among the spectators.19

Hearing the glory of his Lord, Haridasa fell senseless, and his breathing stopped; coming to himself, he roared and burst into dance. The danka withdrew into a corner to give him room. Haridasa rolled on the ground, and the eight sattvika-bhavas appeared in his body; the danka stood with joined palms, and the people took the dust of his feet.

A brahmana by birth grew envious: “Ignorant people honour him because they see him roll in the dust and dance.” He fell to the ground and feigned a swoon, but the danka beat him savagely with a stick, and he ran off howling.

When the danka was asked why he had stood with joined palms before Haridasa and beaten the brahmana, the King of serpents, through the snake charmer's mouth, revealed Haridasa's glory to the people: the brahmana had imitated him out of envy, to steal the honour due to him; the sight of Haridasa dancing cuts worldly bondage, and whoever keeps his company will surely attain Krishna's feet (CB, Adi 16.222–247).20 To display love for Krishna for the sake of honour is ruinous, and even a simple snake charmer sees through the counterfeit.

Chanting Aloud

Before the appearance of Gaurasundara few understood loud chanting. Unbelievers mocked Advaita and Haridasa: the Lord sleeps for the four months of the rains — wake Him and there will be famine; this is how the brahmanas fill their bellies (CB, Adi 16.252–256). It grieved Haridasa, but he did not stop chanting aloud.

In the village of Harinadi (Jessore district) a man who was a brahmana only by birth rudely asked him why he sang the name aloud when it should be repeated silently. Haridasa answered that the scriptures say loud chanting is a hundred times more beneficial than quiet japa, and no scripture condemns it. All beings who hear Krishna's name receive benefit — even a worm that cannot utter it, and in a better birth it will get the chance to serve the Lord:

“Though animals, birds and insects cannot sing, they hear the holy name and so attain liberation. One who repeats Krishna's holy name in a whisper will be liberated; but one who chants the holy name aloud liberates all around him as well. Therefore the scriptures say that one who chants the Lord's name aloud gains a hundred times more benefit.” (CB, Adi 16.280–282)

A verse of the “Naradiya Purana” says the same: “One who chants the names of Hari aloud is a hundred times greater than one who repeats them silently: he purifies both himself and all who hear him.” Quiet japa benefits one person, loud chanting benefits many — just as feeding many is better than feeding oneself alone.

The brahmana flew into a rage: nowadays even the low-born Haridasa has taken to expounding the scriptures; it is said that at the end of the age even shudras will become expounders — and so it has come true.

“If your explanation is not correct, I swear I will cut off your nose and ears.” (CB, Adi 16.295)

“Calmly hearing the sinful brahmana out, Haridasa smiled and began to chant the holy names of the Lord. Without a word to the godless brahmana, he left the assembly of brahmanas, chanting the names of God aloud.” (CB, Adi 16.296–297)

Vrindavana Dasa calls such brahmanas Rakshasas born in brahmana families to persecute the saints (CB, Adi 16.298–300). A few days later that brahmana fell ill with smallpox, and his nose fell off.21

Maya Devi

The “Charitamrita” tells one more story, warning that it cannot be understood by worldly logic but must be heard with faith. On a moonlit night a woman of unheard-of beauty came to Haridasa's cave on the bank of the Ganga: her radiance lit up the courtyard, her fragrance filled all directions. She bowed to the tulasi, circled it, bowed to Haridasa and, sitting at the entrance, began to call him in a voice that could unsettle sages. Haridasa, as once in Benapole, replied that he must first complete his vow of names, and went on chanting. So three nights passed; his mind, absorbed in Krishna and His name, remained unshaken.

At the end of the third night she revealed herself:

“Then, bowing down to him, the woman said, ‘I am Maya. I came to test you. I have bewitched all living beings, beginning with Brahma; you alone I could not bewitch.’” (CC, Antya 3.248–249)

Maya Devi is no demoness-temptress and no defeated enemy, but the Lord's maidservant, who governs His external energy; by His will she came to test His devotee, and she herself received mercy from him. Having heard the name from his lips for three nights, she was purified at heart, accepted him as her guru and fell at his feet:

“‘Long ago I received the name of Rama from Shiva; now, by your company, I long to take the name of Krishna. The name of Rama is the taraka-brahma, the Brahman that delivers, the cause of liberation; the name of Krishna, the paraka, carries one across and gives love. Give me Krishna's name and make me blessed, so that this flood of love may sweep me away too.’” (CC, Antya 3.254–256)

And Haridasa initiated her: “Chant the name of Krishna!” (CC, Antya 3.257). Without the mercy of such a guru and sadhu the soul's chief need — love for Krishna — cannot be attained.

One who chants the name sincerely and without offences cannot be shaken even by Maya herself. But one who, while supposedly taking shelter of the name, yields to women, wealth and fame has not surrendered to the name: the cause is judged by its fruits, and if there are no fruits, the name is being chanted insincerely and with offences.

“Krishna Will Descend”

Advaita worshipped Krishna with Ganga water and tulasi leaves, calling Him into the world, and Haridasa in his cave chanted the name with the same prayer:

“In his cave Haridasa chanted the name, with this one thought in his mind: ‘Krishna will descend.’ By the devotion of these two Chaitanya descended, and by preaching the name and love He delivered the world.” (CC, Antya 3.223–224)22

And then one evening, at the hour of a lunar eclipse, when everyone around was loudly chanting the name of Hari, Advaita in Shantipura guessed that the Lord had appeared; Haridasa understood Him, and both began to dance:

“At that very time, in His own home, Advaita Raya rose and began to dance, joyful at heart. With Haridasa beside Him He roared and sang kirtana in delight — and no one knew why He was dancing.” (CC, Adi 13.99)

Advaita bathed in the Ganga as though for the eclipse and in His mind gave the brahmanas many gifts, and Haridasa, seeing the whole world full of bliss, said to Him in hints that he saw some special cause behind this joy (Adi 13.100–101).

One of the biographies adds that Advaita gave money to the poor and sent gifts to the newborn through Sita, and that what they had understood both kept silent about for the time being.23

With the Lord in Navadvipa

When the Lord returned from Gaya and began His sankirtana, Haridasa settled in Navadvipa, in Advaita's house, to live among pure devotees; from then on Advaita and Haridasa were almost always with the Lord, delighting Him with kirtana. According to one of the biographies, it was then that Haridasa first saw the Lord; before that he had chanted the name now in Mayapur with Advaita, now in his cave in Phulia, now in Shantipura, now in his wanderings.24 Murari Gupta describes how the Lord received him:

“Then He saw the excellent Sri Haridasa — an intoxicated bee at the lotus feet of Sri Krishna, cool and soothing, a festival for the eyes of the saintly, full of grace, like the newly risen moon. Seeing him, Hari of mighty fame embraced this devotee of His feet tightly in both arms and offered him a seat; and he in turn bowed down to Him. At once the Lord anointed him with sandal paste, put a garland on him and gave him mahaprasada — unsurpassed food of the four kinds, full of every flavour; and he ate it at His command.” (“Sri-Krishna-Chaitanya-charitamrita” 2.10.2–4)

Lochana Dasa (“Chaitanya-mangala,” Madhya, 29.59–69) and Kavi Karnapura (mahakavya 7.48–52) tell the same. And on another occasion, Murari says, Haridasa came with a crystal jewel shining on his breast like the moon and with bells on his ankles, and danced beside the Lord (2.10.24); in Lochana Dasa, with a necklace of pure crystal (30.24–27).

The Mahaprakasha

In Srivasa's house the Lord revealed His great manifestation, the Mahaprakasha, which lasted seven praharas, twenty-one hours. He sat on Vishnu's throne, taking the shalagramas to Himself, spoke of His present descent and ate everything that was offered to Him.25 He was worshipped by all the rules — with the recitation of the Rig-veda's “Purusha-sukta,” bathing and arati with five lamps, as one of the biographies relates — and He bestowed boons, calling each devotee by name. Haridasa He called to Himself especially:

“‘O Haridasa, behold My form. You are dearer to Me than My own body; truly you and I are of one caste. When I remember how the Yavanas tormented you, My heart breaks. Listen, Haridasa: when the Yavanas were beating you, leading you from village to village, I saw your suffering and came down from Vaikuntha with the disc in My hand to cut your tormentors to pieces. But you wished them only good, though they had nearly beaten you to death. You paid no heed to the cruel blows and prayed for the welfare of your tormentors. And when you began to pray for their welfare, I could do nothing to them; because of you I could not use My disc. Because of your kindness to them I could not cut off their heads. Seeing with what force and cruelty they were beating you, I covered your back with My own body. I took the blows upon Myself. I speak the truth: look, here are the scars on My back.’” (CB, Madhya 10.35–44)

Hearing this, Haridasa fell senseless; his breathing stopped. The Lord called him: “Get up, My dear Haridasa!” — and, coming to himself, bathed in tears, he rolled about the courtyard for a long time, and then offered the Lord a long prayer: Draupadi, Prahlada and the Pandavas remembered You — and You saved them; but I, a sinner, do not remember You — and yet, Lord, do not abandon me (CB, Madhya 10.52–83).

He asked no other boon than service:

“‘I wish that my food may always be the remnants of Your servants, who tirelessly worship Your lotus feet. <…> O son of Shachi, O my dear one, have mercy on me: let me be a dog in the house of a Vaishnava.’” (CB, Madhya 10.86, 91)

And the Lord granted him:

“The Lord said, ‘Listen, My dear Haridasa. Anyone who lives near you even for a day or hears you even for a moment will surely come to Me; of this there is no doubt. One who shows you respect is in truth honouring Me, for I always dwell in your body.’” (CB, Madhya 10.93–95)26

Vrindavana Dasa closes this account with praise of Haridasa:

“The great Brahma and Shiva always long for the company of devotees like Haridasa. All the gods of this world wish to touch Haridasa, and the holy Ganga waits for Haridasa to bathe in her waters. What to speak of touching Haridasa? Merely seeing him once, a living being casts off forever the chains of material bondage that have bound him since time without beginning.” (CB, Madhya 10.108–110)

Kirtana and Preaching

Every night the Lord sang kirtana with the devotees in Srivasa's house, and sometimes at Chandrashekhara's, and Haridasa was always among them (CB, Madhya 8.110–112). When Nityananda came to Navadvipa, the Lord sent Haridasa and Srivasa to search: “O Haridasa! O Srivasa Pandita! Go and look for anyone who has lately come to the town” (CB, Madhya 3.160) — and for three praharas they went round Navadvipa without finding Him.

Then the Lord made Nityananda and Haridasa the first preachers of the holy name:

“‘Listen, Nityananda! Listen, Haridasa! Go and make My teaching known to the whole world. Go to every house and ask: “Chant Krishna's names, worship Krishna and follow Krishna's teachings.” Speak of nothing else and ask for nothing more. Come at the end of the day and tell Me everything.’” (CB, Madhya 13.8–10)

The housewives, taking them for sannyasis, brought out alms, and they replied: “Our alms are this — serve Krishna, sing His name.” Good people accepted the instruction, others cursed, and those who were not admitted to the night kirtanas in Srivasa's courtyard said that such company had been Nimai Pandita's undoing.

One day they saw two drunken brothers in the street, Jagai and Madhai — by people's account, of a noble brahmana family. Nityananda, wishing to deliver them, said to Haridasa:

“‘O Haridasa, see how wretched they are! Born brahmanas, they have fallen so low; they will never escape the punishment of Yamaraja. When the Yavanas were beating you nearly to death, you cared only for their welfare.’” (CB, Madhya 13.63–65)

The truth about Nityananda was revealed to Haridasa, and he understood that the brothers were already delivered; he replied: “Whatever You desire is the desire of the Lord” (CB, Madhya 13.70–71).

The two preachers approached and repeated the Lord's words to the brothers, but these rushed at them in a fury, and the preachers fled; Haridasa, already old, could hardly keep up with Nityananda. In the evening he complained to Advaita in jest that he would no longer go preaching with Nityananda: He was far too reckless. Later Madhai broke Nityananda's head with a shard of a pot, and the Lord came with the devotees and delivered both brothers.27

Haridasa was with the Lord in His water play in the Ganga after kirtana, too. And when once the Lord in despair threw
Himself into the Ganga, Nityananda and Haridasa pulled Him out. He hid in the house
of Nandana Acharya and told them to keep silent, but later Haridasa brought Srivasa there.

The Kotal of Vaikuntha

In Chandrashekhara's house the Lord staged a drama in which He Himself appeared as Lakshmi, and to Haridasa fell the part of the kotal — the watchman, “the doorkeeper of Vaikuntha.” To Mukunda's kirtana he came out first, in a loincloth and a great turban, staff in hand, and, running round to everyone, roused them with Krishna's name:

“With a flourish Haridasa called out to all: ‘Worship Krishna, serve Krishna, speak Krishna's name!’” (CB, Madhya 18.43)

Everyone laughed and asked who he was and why he had come, and Haridasa disclosed to them the meaning of the drama:

“Haridasa said, ‘I am the kotal of Vaikuntha. At all times I go about awakening Krishna in people. The Lord has left Vaikuntha and come here, and He will freely give away prema-bhakti everywhere. Today He Himself will dance in the dress of Lakshmi — seize prema-bhakti today, and take it with care.’” (CB, Madhya 18.45–47)

Twirling his moustache, he went over to Murari Gupta. So Vrindavana Dasa remembers him: “Haridasa Prabhu called to everyone, ‘Wake up! Wake up!’ and Srivasa Prabhu danced in the dress of Narada” (CB, Madhya 18.100).

And Murari Gupta writes: “Then Haridasa, like the full moon, entered first, a staff in his hand. ‘Sing the kirtana of Hari!’ he proclaimed, awakening the three worlds, which burn with suffering” (“Sri-Krishna-Chaitanya-charitamrita” 2.16.1). In Lochana Dasa he stands in front, staff in hand, and, laughing and shedding tears, calls: “Brothers, perform the sankirtana of Hari's qualities without cease!” (“Chaitanya-mangala,” Madhya, 34.108–109); one of the biographies adds that he burst into dance, twirling his staff, and told everyone to watch attentively. Kavi Karnapura in his drama “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” (Act 3) calls him “Haridasa the stage-manager.” And at the end of the drama the Lord, appearing as the Original Shakti, in Lochana Dasa's words, “taking Haridasa by the hand, smiling, seated him on Her lap,” and he rocked to and fro on Her lap “like a child of five” (34.125–126). This is no disguise and no actor's play, but divine lila: the Lord in the mood of the Mother pours out a mother's tenderness on His devotee.

The Procession to the Kazi's House

On the night of the great procession against the kazi the Lord divided the procession of many thousands into three parts:

“‘Advaita Acharya will dance at the head of the procession, and one of the groups will sing around Him. Haridasa will dance in the middle, and a large group will be around him too. At the rear Srivasa Pandita will dance, and there will be a group around him as well.’” (CB, Madhya 23.141–143)

“Next, obeying the Lord's command, came Haridasa, an ocean of the joy of relationship with Krishna, and his dance was indescribably beautiful.” (CB, Madhya 23.204)28

Last Days in Navadvipa

Once the Lord with Nityananda came unexpectedly to Advaita in Shantipura. The four of them bathed in the Ganga, and when Advaita prostrated Himself at the Lord's feet and Haridasa at Advaita's, it looked like three links of a chain bridge; Nityananda rejoiced, while the Lord was displeased that Advaita had bowed at His feet. A few days later the Lord returned to Navadvipa with Nityananda and Haridasa (CB, Madhya 19). Murari Gupta says that in Advaita's abode the Lord “was full of mercy towards Haridasa” (3.18.17).

On another evening the Lord came with Haridasa to Murari's house and privately instructed Murari to serve Advaita (Murari 2.18.25–26; “Chaitanya-mangala,” Madhya, 38.53).

His decision to take sannyasa the Lord concealed from everyone except Nityananda — even from Haridasa, so that his grief would not become inconsolable. The day before, Haridasa was at His house, and on the last night Haridasa and Gadadhara slept near the Lord; waking, they did not find Him. Advaita and Haridasa went away to Shantipura.

Farewell in Shantipura

Having taken sannyasa, the Lord came to Advaita in Shantipura; He had said beforehand that He would come there “by way of Haridasa Thakura's Phulia.” In the evening kirtana began:

“Nityananda Gosani moved along with the Acharya, holding Him, and behind them Haridasa danced for joy.” (CC, Madhya 3.113)

When the Lord called Haridasa and Mukunda to share His meal, both declined:

“Haridasa said, ‘I am most sinful and lowly. Later I shall eat a handful outside.’” (CC, Madhya 3.63)29

And when the Lord had eaten, He Himself asked Advaita to go and eat with Mukunda and Haridasa, and Advaita gladly did as He had wished in His heart (CC, Madhya 3.106–107).

The Lord was about to leave for Puri, and Haridasa grieved: how could he live in separation, since one born in a Muslim family would not be admitted to Jagannatha's temple, and Orissa and Bengal were then at war?

“When He had bidden them all farewell, the Lord made up His mind to set out. Then Haridasa, weeping, spoke piteously: ‘You will go to Nilachala — but what will become of me? I have no power to go there. Lowly as I am, I shall not be able to see You. How shall I keep this sinful life?’ The Lord said, ‘Restrain your humility; it troubles My heart. For your sake I shall plead with Jagannatha, and I shall take you with Me to Sri Purushottama.’” (CC, Madhya 3.193–197)

Murari Gupta and Lochana Dasa tell that Haridasa, holding a straw between his teeth, threw himself at the Lord's feet, and the Lord with tears Himself longed to fall at Jagannatha's feet (“Chaitanya-mangala,” Madhya, 42.11–15); in Murari He answers: “In just this way I Myself will fall at the lotus feet of Jagannatha and plead that the mercy of Hari will surely rest upon you” (Murari 3.4.29–30).

Siddha-bakula

Returning from the South, the Lord sent Kala Krishnadasa to Bengal with a message for the devotees: let them come, led by Advaita, to the Ratha-yatra. To Haridasa He sent word to come and live at His feet for the rest of his life; the message brought Haridasa back to life. He came to Puri with the devotees of Gauda — and stayed there for good.

The Lord came out to meet two hundred devotees, embraced each one and asked, “Where is Haridasa?” But Haridasa lay prostrate at the edge of the road, far from everyone.

“Haridasa said, ‘I am low-born and worthless. I have no right to go near the temple. If I can get a secluded place within the garden, I will stay there alone and pass my days. There I shall not come into contact with the servants of Jagannatha. To stay there is my desire.’” (CC, Madhya 11.165–167)

The Lord was pleased with his words and asked Kashi Mishra for a secluded hut in a flower garden not far from His own residence. Then He Himself came to Haridasa:

“Seeing the Lord, he fell prostrate at His feet, and the Lord raised him up and embraced him. Both of them wept, absorbed in love: the servant overcome by the master's virtues, and the master by the servant's. Haridasa said, ‘O Lord, do not touch me. I am low, untouchable, the most fallen of all.’ The Lord said, ‘I touch you to purify Myself, for I have none of your pure dharma. At every moment you bathe in all the holy places; at every moment you perform sacrifice, austerity and charity. You study the Vedas without cease, and you are far more purifying than any brahmana or sannyasi.’” (CC, Madhya 11.186–191)

“So saying, He took him to the flower garden and gave him a dwelling in a very secluded spot. ‘Stay here and sing the holy Name. I shall come and meet you every day. When you see the chakra on the temple, offer your obeisance. Your prasada will be brought to you here.’” (CC, Madhya 11.193–195)

This place, behind the Gambhira where the Lord lived, is now called Siddha-bakula: an ancient bakula tree grew there. According to a tradition given by one of the biographies, the temple priests gave the Lord a bakula twig with which Jagannatha's “teeth were cleaned,” and He planted it by the place of Haridasa's bhajana; in time the twig became a large tree. This, they say, was on Chaitra's first day, at Mahavishuva-sankranti, and on that day the Danta-kashtha-ropana, “the planting of the toothstick,” is celebrated there every year; formerly the garden was called the Mudra Matha.30

No one forbade Haridasa to enter the temple, but out of humility he never entered either it or Kashi Mishra's house; so too, later, did Rupa and Sanatana:

“Haridasa Thakura, Sri Rupa and Sanatana — these three did not go into the temple of Jagannatha. After seeing Jagannatha's upala-bhoga offering, Mahaprabhu would meet these three and then go to His own residence. Whichever of the three was there at the time, the Lord would come and meet him Himself — this was His rule.” (CC, Madhya 1.63–65)

And every day, when food was offered to Jagannatha, the Lord came out of the temple to Haridasa:

“When the upala-bhoga began, He would come out of the temple, meet Haridasa, and return to His own dwelling.” (CC, Madhya 15.6)

Govinda, the Lord's servant, brought him the remnants of the Lord's meal every day. Such was the humility of the Namacharya: he did not enter the temple, did not sit to eat with the devotees, lay prostrate at the roadside.

When the Gundicha temple had been cleaned and the water pastimes in Narendra Lake were over, the Lord fed the devotees in the garden and called Haridasa again and again to the meal, but he answered from afar:

“‘Let the Lord take prasada with the devotees. Worthless as I am, I am not fit to sit in this company. Later Govinda will give me prasada outside the gate.’ Knowing his mind, the Lord did not call him again.” (CC, Madhya 12.161–162)

At the Ratha-yatra the Lord divided the kirtana into groups and appointed a dancer in each: Nityananda, Advaita, Haridasa and Vakreshvara (CC, Madhya 13.35).

“He formed another group with Mukunda as the leader, in which Vasudeva, Gopinatha and Murari sang, with two more, Shrikanta and Vallabha Sena; and Haridasa Thakura danced there.” (CC, Madhya 13.40–41)

One of the biographies adds that Jagannatha Himself, charmed by the Lord's dancing, halted His chariot to see it. And at the Gundicha temple the Lord had now Advaita, now Nityananda, now Haridasa dance (CC, Madhya 14.71).31

The residents of Puri and the Lord's constant companions became close to him: “Gadadhara Pandita Gosani lived in Nilachala, as did Vakreshvara, Damodara, Shankara and Haridasa” (CC, Madhya 1.252). Jagadananda Pandita came to know him in Puri; Damodara Pandita, coming to Siddha-bakula, met the Namacharya and was overjoyed; Svarupa, Ramananda and Haridasa honoured the feet of Nityananda.

Ramakeli

Haridasa was also among the Lord's companions when He set out for Vrindavana through Bengal and reached Ramakeli. There Rupa and Sanatana, still in the service of the ruler of Gauda, came secretly to the Lord at night:

“At midnight the two brothers came to where the Lord was staying. First they met Nityananda and Haridasa. These two told the Lord: ‘Rupa and Sakara Mallika have come to see You.’” (CC, Madhya 1.183–184)

The Lord told His companions, Haridasa among them, to bless the brothers. And Sanatana advised the Lord not to go further with such a crowd: the Muslim ruler could not be trusted, and it did not befit a pilgrim to lead thousands of people behind him (CC, Madhya 1.222–224); and the Lord turned back.32 It was then, according to one of the biographies, that Rupa and Sanatana first met Haridasa and came to know one another's virtues well; that friendship later continued in Puri, in Haridasa's hut.

Rupa and Sanatana in Haridasa's Hut

When Rupa Gosvami came to Puri from Vrindavana, he stayed with Haridasa, who received him lovingly: “The Lord has already told me that you would come.” Soon the Lord came to them unexpectedly, embraced Rupa, seated the two side by side and questioned them at length (CC, Antya 1). Govinda brought them the remnants of the Lord's meal:

“All the devotees were eating prasada and calling out ‘Hari!’ Seeing this, Haridasa and Rupa were delighted. Through Govinda they received the remnants of the Lord's meal, and the two of them, intoxicated with love, began to dance.” (CC, Antya 1.63–64)

The leaf with the verse “priyah so 'yam” Rupa tucked under the thatched roof of Haridasa's hut, and there the Lord found it. And when the Lord recited Rupa's verse about the holy name, “tunde tandavini” — “it dances on the tongue,” Haridasa began to dance:

“Hearing the verse, Haridasa was jubilant, and he began to dance, praising its meaning. ‘I know the glory of Krishna's name from the scriptures and from the lips of saints, but nowhere have I heard of such sweetness in the name.’” (CC, Antya 1.100–101)

The Lord came to Rupa at Haridasa's dwelling with Ramananda Raya, Svarupa Damodara and Sarvabhauma, and when the devotees of Gauda arrived, Advaita, Nityananda, Haridasa and the others embraced Rupa.

Rupa and Sanatana, though of brahmana birth, regarded themselves as untouchable because they had served at the court of a Muslim ruler, and, fearing to touch the servants of Jagannatha, they lived with Haridasa; when the Lord came, He embraced Haridasa and whichever of the brothers was there.

Sanatana came to Puri covered with sores, found Haridasa's dwelling and bowed to him; Haridasa embraced him and asked him to live there with him. The Lord told Sanatana to remain with Haridasa, sent them prasada through Govinda and entrusted Haridasa with the care of Sanatana's body. Once the Lord said that Sanatana's body was His own, and Haridasa exclaimed, “There is no limit to your good fortune!” But Sanatana answered:

“Sanatana said, ‘Who else is there like you? Among Mahaprabhu's associates you are the most fortunate! The Lord descended to spread the name, and He accomplishes this, His own work, through you. <…> You do both works for the name — practice (achara) and preaching (prachara). You are the guru of all; you are the noblest in the world.’” (CC, Antya 4.99–100, 103)

When the Lord praised Sanatana, Haridasa objected that this was only outward: the Lord is compassionate to the fallen and therefore accepted them (CC, Antya 4.181–182). The Lord answered them with a smile, “Listen, Haridasa and Sanatana! <…> I regard you all as My children,” and a mother feels no disgust for her child (CC, Antya 4.183–187). Haridasa replied:

“‘You are the Lord, full of mercy. No one can understand Your deep heart. Vasudeva was a leper with oozing sores, his body full of worms, yet out of compassion You embraced him. By embracing him You made his body as beautiful as Kandarpa's. We cannot understand the waves of Your mercy.’” (CC, Antya 4.188–190)

And the Lord revealed: “A Vaishnava's body is never material” (CC, Antya 4.191). Sanatana lived with Haridasa in Nilachala, and they spoke endlessly of the Lord.33

Talks on the Holy Name

In Siddha-bakula the Lord, to reveal the glory of the name to the world, questioned Haridasa. Once He asked how in the age of Kali the Yavanas would be delivered, who are strangers to the Vedas and do violence to cows and brahmanas.

“Haridasa said, ‘Lord, do not worry. Do not grieve at the sight of the Yavanas' worldly bondage. All the Yavanas will attain liberation easily, for they say “ha rama, ha rama,” and so they utter the semblance of the name (namabhasa). In great love a devotee cries, “Ha Rama! Ha Rama!” See the good fortune of the Yavanas: they utter that very name! When the name is uttered to point to something else, that is namabhasa; yet even then the potency of the name is not destroyed.’” (CC, Antya 3.52–55)

And he cited a verse of the “Nrisimha Purana”: a mleccha struck by a boar's tusk who cries “haram!” attains liberation by that alone (Antya 3.56); and Ajamila, dying, called his son, “Narayana!” — and the messengers of Vishnu drove away the messengers of Yama (Antya 3.57, 3.63). Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura explains that a Muslim who dies with the word “haram” on his lips is liberated, for that word contains the Lord's name, even though spoken of something else (nama-sanketa).34 The semblance of the name (namabhasa) gives liberation; love for Krishna, prema, is given by the pure name.

“And how will the nonmoving and moving beings be delivered?” the Lord asked.

“Haridasa said, ‘Lord, that is by Your mercy: You have already delivered the nonmoving and moving beings. You have performed this loud sankirtana, and the nonmoving and moving beings have all heard it. By hearing it, the moving beings are freed from worldly existence; and when that sound strikes the nonmoving beings, an echo arises. It is not an “echo”: they are performing “kirtana.”’” (CC, Antya 3.67–70)

Balabhadra Bhattacharya, the Lord's only companion on the way to Vrindavana, had told Haridasa how in the forests of Jharikhanda tigers and elephants let them pass, while deer and peacocks danced side by side with the tigers, repeating “Krishna, Krishna,” and, forgetting their enmity, embraced one another (Antya 3.72).

“But if all beings are delivered, will the universe not be emptied?” Haridasa replied that as long as the Lord is in this world He will send all souls to Vaikuntha, while other souls will come into the world again and fill the universe as before — just as Ramachandra took all Ayodhya with Him and peopled it anew (Antya 3.76–80). Delighted, the Lord then glorified Haridasa's virtues before the devotees.

Krishnadasa Kaviraja sums it up:

“Through Haridasa He revealed the glory of the holy name; through Sanatana, the conclusions of bhakti in all their splendour.” (CC, Antya 5.86)

And the “Bhakti-ratnakara” says: “Through Haridasa He showed forbearance, through Sanatana and Rupa He revealed humility” (1.631).

And the Lord Himself told Vallabha Bhatta that it was from Haridasa that He had learned the glory of the name:

“Haridasa Thakura is the foremost of the great bhagavatas. Every day he chants three lakhs (three hundred thousand) of names. From him I learned the glory of the holy name; by his grace that glory was revealed to Me.” (CC, Antya 7.46–47)

The Departure

Years passed. One day Govinda brought Haridasa mahaprasada and found him lying down, very slowly chanting his names. Haridasa said that today he was fasting, as his number of names was not complete — but, so as not to disregard the mahaprasada, he bowed to it and ate a single grain (CC, Antya 11.16–20).

The next day the Lord came and asked whether he was well. “My body is well,” Haridasa replied, “but my mind is not: I cannot complete my vow.” The Lord said:

“‘You have grown old; reduce the number of your names. You are ever perfect, even in body; why are you so intent on sadhana? You have descended to deliver the people, and you have preached the glory of the holy name in the world.’” (CC, Antya 11.24–25)

Then Haridasa disclosed a long-held desire. The Lord, he said, had accepted him, low-born as he was, as His servant and raised him from hell to Vaikuntha, and he understood that the Lord would soon wind up His pastimes in this world:

“‘Lord, never let me see that pastime. Let my body fall before You. I shall hold Your lotus feet to my heart and gaze with my eyes upon Your moonlike face. With my tongue I shall utter Your name, “Krishna Chaitanya.” This is my desire — to give up my life in this way.’” (CC, Antya 11.32–34)35

This was neither fear of death nor flight from service: Haridasa did not wish to see the Lord disappear.

The Lord replied that merciful Krishna would grant whatever he asked, but all the Lord's own happiness lay in his company. Haridasa, clasping His feet, begged Him not to play tricks: the Lord had millions of devotees, and if one insect like him were gone, what would the world lose (CC, Antya 11.37–42)? The Lord, though saddened by the coming separation, granted his wish.

In the morning, after seeing Jagannatha, the Lord came to him with all the devotees. “Haridasa, what news?” “Lord, as You command.” A great kirtana began in the courtyard. Before Ramananda Raya, Sarvabhauma and all the devotees the Lord, as if five-mouthed, glorified Haridasa's virtues, and all bowed to his feet (CC, Antya 11.45–52).

“Haridasa seated the Lord in front of himself and fixed his eyes, like two bees, on the lotus of His face. He brought the Lord's feet to his heart and held them there; the dust of the feet of all the devotees adorned his head. Again and again he said, ‘Sri Krishna Chaitanya Prabhu!’ He drank in the sweetness of the Lord's face, and streams of tears flowed from his eyes. And so, as he uttered the words ‘Sri Krishna Chaitanya,’ he let his life go forth from his body together with the name. Like a great master of yoga, he departed at his own will, and everyone remembered the departure of Bhishma.” (CC, Antya 11.53–57)36

So the Namacharya left this world — by his own will, with the Lord's name on his lips, gazing at His face. Brahmanas by birth bowed to him and placed his feet on their heads: a Vaishnava is worthy of honour, whatever family he was born in.

Svarupa Damodara and the devotees sang the name around Haridasa, Vakreshvara Pandita danced, and when Haridasa had gone, the Lord took his body in His arms and danced with it all around the courtyard (CC, Antya 11.48–49, 59). With this Kaviraja opens his account of Haridasa's departure:

“I bow to Haridasa and to his Lord, Chaitanya, who took the body of the departed Haridasa on His lap and danced.” (CC, Antya 11.1)

The “Advaita-prakasha” (19.142–154) and the “Gaura-krishnodaya” (17.42–46) tell the same.

The Samadhi

The body was carried to the sea on a palanquin shaped like a celestial chariot; the Lord went in front, dancing, and Vakreshvara and the devotees sang and danced behind.37

“He bathed Haridasa in the water of the sea and said, ‘This sea has now become a great holy place (maha-tirtha).’” (CC, Antya 11.64)

The devotees drank the water in which his feet had been bathed and anointed his body with sandal paste, the prasada of Jagannatha.

A pit was dug in the sand and the body laid in it, adorned with Jagannatha's prasada — silk cords, sandal paste, food and cloth.

“Calling ‘Hari bol! Hari bol!’, Gauraraya Himself put sand on Haridasa's body with His holy hands.” (CC, Antya 11.68)

The devotees covered the body with sand and raised a platform with an enclosure over it; the Lord circled the samadhi, sang and danced, and the sound of kirtana filled all Puri. So the Lord Himself performed the samadhi of His devotee, and by his presence the seashore became a great tirtha. A Vaishnava's body is not material, and this was no funeral but a festival of departure — a niryana-mahotsava.

At the Lion Gate of the temple the Lord spread the end of His upper cloth and asked the shopkeepers for prasada:

“‘I am begging prasada for the festival of Haridasa Thakura. Please give Me alms.’” (CC, Antya 11.74)

The shopkeepers joyfully brought their baskets, but Svarupa Damodara sent the Lord home and collected the prasada himself. The Lord began to serve it Himself, lavishly, enough for five on each leaf, but Svarupa seated Him, and the serving was done by Svarupa, Jagadananda, Kashishvara and Shankara (Antya 11.75–84).38 At the festival were Paramananda Puri, Ramananda Raya, Sarvabhauma and all the devotees.

When everyone had eaten, the Lord adorned each with a garland and sandal paste and gave His blessing:

“‘Whoever saw the festival of Haridasa's departure, whoever danced here or sang kirtana, whoever went to put sand on him, and whoever among them ate at the festival — all of them will soon attain Krishna. Such is the power of seeing Haridasa. Out of mercy Krishna gave Me Haridasa's company. Krishna's will is independent: now He has broken that company. When Haridasa wished to go, My power could not keep him. By his wish alone he sent his life forth from his body, as we have heard Bhishma did long ago. Haridasa was the crest jewel of the earth; without him the earth has been robbed of its jewel.’” (CC, Antya 11.91–97)

And the Lord cried, “Glory to Haridasa Thakura!” and began to dance, while the devotees answered, “Glory, glory, glory to Haridasa, who revealed the glory of the holy name!” (Antya 11.98–99). Kaviraja concludes that whoever hears of Haridasa's departure gains firm devotion to Krishna (Antya 11.101).

After Haridasa's departure the Lord's ecstasies grew stronger day by day.

The day of Haridasa Thakura's departure is observed in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math on the Gaura-chaturdashi of the month of Hrishikesha (in 2026, on 25 September); one of the biographies names the same tithi — the shukla-chaturdashi of the month of Bhadra. No source names the year of his departure; it is clear only that he left shortly before the Lord's disappearance.39

The Place of Remembrance

The samadhi of Haridasa Thakura stands on the seashore in Puri. After the Lord's disappearance Srinivasa Acharya came to it and grieved there in separation (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 3.222–228); on the advice of Gopinatha Acharya, Narottama Dasa Thakura visited the samadhi (“Narottama-vilasa” 4). According to the “Prema-vivarta” (ch. 19), it was at Haridasa's samadhi that the Lord expounded the “Nama-rahasya-patala.”

Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura wrote in English the “Slokas of Hari Das Thakur's Samadhi” (1871). In 1900 Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati wished to perform his bhajana at Haridasa's samadhi, and he was entrusted with the service of Giridhari at the Satasan Matha; in 1902 “Bhakti Kuti” was built nearby. On 15 July 1951 Srila Bhakti Vilasa Tirtha Maharaja laid the foundation of Sri Purushottama Gaudiya Math by Haridasa's samadhi.

In 1905 in Mayapur Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, following Haridasa Thakura, vowed to chant a billion names — not less than three lakhs a day. And speaking of the body of Srila Gaurakishora Dasa Babaji after his departure, Bhaktisiddhanta recalled: “When Haridasa entered the eternal pastimes, Gauranga held his body to His breast and danced.” Haridasa's departure and the festival in his honour are the model of how to honour the departure of a perfect Vaishnava.

The “Narottama-vilasa” (ch. 7) tells that at the festival in Kheturi Mahaprabhu, Nityananda, Advaita, Haridasa and other associates, long since departed from the world, appeared again in the sankirtana.

Haridasa's name appears in many other accounts of the original sources — among those who danced at the festival of Madhavendra Puri (CB, Antya 4), who rejoiced with Achyuta and Sita at Advaita's embraces, among whom Lokanatha saw the Lord, whom Shachi gladdened in Shantipura, and in the lists of associates in Murari Gupta and Lochana Dasa; Gangadasa and Srivasa explained to him and Nityananda who Jagai and Madhai were; Vasudeva Datta, according to the “Anubhashya,” showed the same boundless compassion as Haridasa; and Srila Bhakti Prajnan Yati Maharaja was inspired by his life from childhood, and above all by the words “Even if my body is cut to pieces…” (CB, Adi 16.94).

In Narahari Chakravarti's “Namamrita-samudra,” where the Lord's associates are invoked one after another, Haridasa is given the third verse — right after the Pancha-tattva:

“Haridasa, ocean of mercy, dear to Gaura! Make the holy Name manifest in my sinful heart.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 3)

Significance

Haridasa Thakura is Brahma and Prahlada, an eternal associate sent into the world before the Lord. Through him the Lord revealed the glory of the holy name, and his very life was a preaching of the name: in deed — three hundred thousand names every day; in word — loud chanting and the teaching on namabhasa. That is why Sanatana called him the guru of the whole world.

The Lord deliberately had him born among Muslims to show that a Vaishnava is not defined by birth and that every devotee is worthy of honour. Brahmanas bowed at his feet, Advaita gave him the shraddha-patra, and the Lord called him purer than any brahmana or sannyasi. Haridasa himself considered himself lower than all and would not even enter the temple.

His life teaches that a Vaishnava bears no grudge against anyone and prays even for his executioners, but that Krishna does not tolerate offences against His devotees. It teaches too that without the mercy of such a sadhu love for Krishna cannot be attained: the prostitute, Maya Devi and the boy Raghunatha received it from him. And the Lord Himself promised: whoever lives near Haridasa even for a day or hears him even for a moment will surely come to Him.
